text:
The problem asks for the smallest constant \(C\) such that, no matter how the \(2025\) people distribute their unit‑mass among the \(66\) colors, we can select one ball per person so that for each color the total selected mass is at most \(C\).

For a fixed weight matrix \((w_{i,c})\) the selector’s task is equivalent to a load‑balancing problem: we must assign each person to a color \(c\) and then the load on color \(c\) is \(L_c=\sum_{i:\sigma(i)=c} w_{i,c}\).  
If the adversary makes all people identical, i.e. \(w_{i,c}=w_c\) for all \(i\), the selector only chooses how many people \(n_c\) to send to each color. The constraint \(L_c\le C\) becomes \(n_c w_c\le C\).  

For a given weight vector \(w\) the smallest achievable \(C\) is the minimum \(L\) for which the integer capacities
\[
\bigl\lfloor \tfrac{L}{w_c}\bigr\rfloor\qquad(c=1,\dots ,66)
\]
allow us to place all \(2025\) people, i.e.
\[
\sum_{c=1}^{66} \Bigl\lfloor \tfrac{L}{w_c}\Bigr\rfloor \;\ge\;2025 .
\]
If we set all weights equal, \(w_c=\tfrac1{66}\), then the capacity of each color is \(\bigl\lfloor 66L\bigr\rfloor\).  
To cover the 2025 people we need
\[
66\bigl\lfloor 66L\bigr\rfloor \ge 2025 .
\]
The smallest integer \(k\) with \(66k\ge2025\) is \(k=31\) (since \(66\cdot30=1980<2025\) and \(66\cdot31=2046\ge2025\)). Hence we must have \(\lfloor 66L\rfloor\ge31\), which forces \(L\ge\frac{31}{66}\).

With \(L=\frac{31}{66}\) we can assign at most \(31\) people to each color; the total capacity is \(66\cdot31=2046\), more than enough for the 2025 people, so a feasible assignment exists. Any smaller \(L\) would give capacity at most \(30\) per color and total capacity \(1980<2025\), which is insufficient. Therefore the optimal constant is
\[
C_{\min}= \frac{31}{66}.
\]

The proposed solution yields \(C=\frac{992}{2069}\approx0.4798\), which is strictly larger than the optimal value \(31/66\approx0.4697\). Hence the answer is not optimal.

**Verdict:** REJECT.
